item.title: … (At Sāvatthi). Standing to one side, that deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One: As if struck by a sword,…
item.description:
… (At Sāvatthi). Standing to one side, that deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
As if struck by a sword,
As if fire blazed on the head —
Mindful, a monk should go forth,
Abandoning lust for sensual pleasures.

(The Blessed One):
As if struck by a sword,
As if fire blazed on the head —
Mindful, a monk should go forth,
Abandoning identity view.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.21
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Thus, monks, a clansman goes forth. He has desire for sensual pleasures, ardent craving, a mind of ill-will, defiled thoughts, lacking mindfulness, not clearly comprehending,…
item.description:
“Thus, monks, a clansman goes forth. He has desire for sensual pleasures, ardent craving, a mind of ill-will, defiled thoughts, lacking mindfulness, not clearly comprehending, not concentrated, with distracted mind, with uncontrolled faculties. Monks, like a charnel-fire brand that is burning at both ends and smeared with feces in the middle, not used as fuel in the village nor in the forest — with that simile, I describe that person, who has lost both the householder’s enjoyment and the goal of the ascetic life.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.80
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, these nine perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, having the deathless as their end. What…
item.description:
“Monks, these nine perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, having the deathless as their end. What nine? The perception of foulness, the perception of death, the perception of disgust with food, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in impermanence, the perception of not-self in suffering, the perception of abandoning, the perception of dispassion. These nine perceptions, monks, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, having the deathless as their end.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.16
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Form is like a lump of foam, Feeling like a water bubble, Perception like a mirage, Formations like a banana tree, Consciousness like a magic…
item.description:
Form is like a lump of foam,
Feeling like a water bubble,
Perception like a mirage,
Formations like a banana tree,
Consciousness like a magic trick —
So taught the Kinsman of the Sun.

If one reflects appropriately,
And rightly examines,
Seeing things as they really are,
Emptiness is clearly seen.

Beginning with this body,
As taught by the Great Sage,
When three things are abandoned,
Form is seen as discarded.

This body is discarded, unaware,
Not feeling, just heat and consciousness —
When thrown away, it lies,
Food for others.

This continuous body,
A magic trick, said the fool,
Is called a murderer —
No core can be found.

Thus should a monk contemplate the aggregates,
Ardent,
Both by day and by night,
Mindful and clearly comprehending.

He should abandon all fetters,
Make a refuge for himself,
Live as if his head were on fire,
Aspiring to the imperturbable state.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.95
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, those ascetics or brahmins who are not tied, infatuated, or utterly committed to these five strands of sensual pleasure, who see their peril, who…
item.description:
“Monks, those ascetics or brahmins who are not tied, infatuated, or utterly committed to these five strands of sensual pleasure, who see their peril, who know the escape from them, and who enjoy them—they should be understood as not fallen into misfortune, not fallen into calamity, and are not being used by Māra as he wishes. Monks, just as a forest deer that has not fallen into a trap does not have to lie down—that deer should be understood as not fallen into misfortune, not fallen into calamity, and is not being used by the hunter as he wishes. When the hunter comes, the deer can leave as it wishes. So too, monks, those ascetics or brahmins who are not tied … are not being used by Māra as he wishes.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 26 – Ariyapariyesanāsutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, desire and lust for the eye is a defilement of the mind. Desire and lust for the ear … for the nose … for…
item.description:
“Monks, desire and lust for the eye is a defilement of the mind. Desire and lust for the ear … for the nose … for the tongue … for the body … for the mind is a defilement of the mind. When a monk has abandoned these defilements in regard to these six sense bases, his mind inclines to renunciation. Having been fully saturated with renunciation, his mind becomes wieldy and he directly knows the things to be fully known.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 27.1
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “So too, Māgandiya, if I were to teach you the Dhamma thus: ‘This is health, this is Nibbāna,’ you might know health and see Nibbāna.…
item.description:
“So too, Māgandiya, if I were to teach you the Dhamma thus: ‘This is health, this is Nibbāna,’ you might know health and see Nibbāna. And with the arising of the eye (of wisdom) in you, lust for the five aggregates of clinging would be abandoned, and you might think: ‘For a long time indeed I have been deceived, cheated, and fooled by this mind! For I clung to form, I clung to feeling, I clung to perception, I clung to formations, I clung to consciousness. Because of that clinging, there is becoming for me; because of becoming, birth; because of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.’”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 75 – Māgandiyasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “And what, monks, is the peril in the case of feelings? Feelings are impermanent, suffering, subject to change – that is the peril in the…
item.description:
“And what, monks, is the peril in the case of feelings? Feelings are impermanent, suffering, subject to change – that is the peril in the case of feelings. And what, monks, is the escape in the case of feelings? The removal of desire and lust for feelings, the abandoning of desire and lust – that is the escape in the case of feelings.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 13 – Mahādukkhakkhandhasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “What do you think, prince? For that householder or householder’s son, do bodily or mental fevers arise due to craving? Burned by those fevers born…
item.description:
“What do you think, prince? For that householder or householder’s son, do bodily or mental fevers arise due to craving? Burned by those fevers born of craving, does he experience suffering?” - “Yes, venerable sir.” - “That householder or householder’s son, prince, burned by fevers born of craving, experiences suffering. That craving has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, made non-existent, unable to arise in the future. Therefore I feel at ease.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.35
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, thus I have opened the safe, secure path leading to happiness, closed the dangerous path, removed the male decoy, destroyed the female decoy. Monks,…
item.description:
“Monks, thus I have opened the safe, secure path leading to happiness, closed the dangerous path, removed the male decoy, destroyed the female decoy. Monks, whatever a teacher should do for his disciples out of compassion, that I have done for you out of compassion. Monks, here are the roots of trees, here are empty places. Meditate, do not be heedless, do not have cause for regret later. This is my instruction to you.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 19 – Dvedhāvitakkasutta
📖 Read this sutta
